summary: Defines jCal, a JSON format for iCalendar data. iCalendar is the text format for events and tasks in calendar applications, and JSON is a common lightweight data format.

eli5.summary: Calendars are normally saved in one kind of text. This writes the same events in another common style so web programs can use it more easily.

questions: how does jcal represent icalendar properties
what is the jcal media type
how are recurrence rules written in jcal
subtitle: A one-to-one mapping that lets calendar events and tasks travel as ordinary JSON arrays and objects.

tldr.problem: iCalendar is a specialized text format that needs its own parser and generator, while JSON is the native format of JavaScript widgets and libraries.
tldr.mechanism: jCal maps each iCalendar component, property, parameter and value to a JSON array, object or primitive, so data can be converted to JSON and back without losing meaning.
tldr.outcome: Applications get calendar data in a form that is easier to handle, and the RFC registers the media type application/calendar+json. It has since been updated by RFC 7529.

today: RFC 7265 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 7529, so read the two together.

sections.title: Why a JSON Form of iCalendar
sections.content:
The iCalendar format (RFC 5545) is a widely deployed way to exchange calendaring and scheduling data. It is also a specialized format, so every application that touches it needs its own parser and generator. JSON, defined in RFC 7159, is the native format for JavaScript widgets and libraries, so a standard JSON form of calendar data is easier to work with.

jCal is that form. It is a straightforward mapping, so iCalendar data can be converted to JSON and back again without losing any semantic meaning. The design goals copy those of xCal, the XML format in RFC 6321: round-tripping gives the same semantic result, ordering and the case of names are not necessarily preserved, and extensions to iCalendar must not require an update to jCal.

A simple consumer can browse the data in jCal, but a full understanding of iCalendar is still needed to modify it.
sections.eli5: Calendar files are written in a special style that few programs read easily. jCal rewrites the same information in a style that web programs already know, and it can be turned back without losing anything.

sections.title: Components, Properties and Parameters
sections.content:
An iCalendar object is made of components, properties, parameters and values. jCal gives each one a JSON shape. The top level is a jCal object, which is the component vcalendar. There is no equivalent of an iCalendar stream, but several objects can be carried in a plain JSON array.

A component, delimited by BEGIN and END in iCalendar, becomes a fixed-length array of three fields: its name in lowercase, an array of properties, and an array of sub-components. This applies to current components and to any added later. The original order of properties and sub-components is not kept, but the meaning is.

A property is an array with three fixed elements followed by its values: the lowercase property name, an object holding the parameters (an empty object if there are none), and a lowercase type identifier for the value. A single-valued property therefore has exactly four elements, and a multi-valued property such as categories has one more element per value. Parsers must check the type identifier and not rely on the property name alone.

Parameters are a JSON object whose keys are the lowercase parameter names, with the case of the values preserved. Parameters that allow a comma-separated list become an array of strings, and a single-valued one may be either a string or a one-element array, so a parser MUST accept both. The VALUE parameter is never put in the object. The value type is signaled by the third element of the property instead.

Two properties are special. geo becomes an array of two numbers, latitude then longitude. request-status becomes an array of two or three strings (code, description and, if present, extra data). Converting back, the values MUST be joined with a semicolon.
sections.eli5: Think of a labeled box with a list of smaller boxes inside. Each calendar item becomes a short list: its name, some extra notes, its kind, and then the actual value.

sections.title: How Each Value Type Is Written
sections.content:
Each iCalendar value type gets a lowercase type identifier and a JSON form. Text, URIs and calendar user addresses are JSON strings. Booleans are JSON booleans, floats and integers are JSON numbers, and binary data stays a base64 string. Integers MUST resolve to an integer in the range RFC 5545 allows.

Dates and times are where jCal differs most. They use the extended format of ISO 8601, with hyphens and colons, as in 2011-05-17 and 2012-10-17T12:00:00Z. Reduced-accuracy forms MUST NOT be used. A UTC offset keeps the iCalendar value but puts a colon between the hour and minute, as in -05:00. Durations keep their iCalendar form, such as P1D.

A period is an array of two strings: a date-time start, and an end that is either a date-time or a duration. A recur value, the recurrence rule, becomes a JSON object. Rule part names are lowercase. freq and wkst are strings, until is a date or date-time, count and interval are single numbers, and parts that can have several values, such as bymonthday or byday, are arrays. A single-valued part may be a bare value or a one-element array, and a parser MUST understand both.
sections.eli5: Each kind of thing gets its own way of being written down. Numbers are numbers, yes or no is true or false, and dates use dashes the way many web programs expect.

sections.title: Converting in Each Direction
sections.content:
Converting iCalendar to jCal happens in a fixed order. First, folded lines (iCalendar wraps long lines, typically at 75 octets) MUST be unfolded. Then iCalendar escaping MUST be removed, and finally JSON escaping MUST be applied. Converting back reverses the order: JSON escaping is removed, iCalendar escaping is applied as defined by RFC 5545 and RFC 6868, and long lines SHOULD be folded.

Base64 needs care. If a property has ENCODING=BASE64 and its type is BINARY, the encoding is kept. For any other type the ENCODING parameter MUST be removed and the value decoded. Converting back, non-binary values MUST NOT be base64 encoded.

Names go to uppercase again on the way back: components, properties and parameters SHOULD be converted to uppercase, which is common practice even though iCalendar names are case insensitive. The VALUE parameter is added when the jCal type differs from the property default, and it MAY be omitted when the type is the default.
sections.eli5: It is like translating a letter and back: you do the steps in one order going there and the opposite order coming home, so nothing gets scrambled.

sections.title: Unknown Properties and Extensions
sections.content:
Extension properties and parameters, the ones starting with X-, are handled exactly like any other: the name is lowercased and the shape is the same, so X-FOO becomes x-foo. The difficulty is that a converter may not know the default value type of a new or extension property, and guessing would break round-tripping.

For this, jCal adds an unknown value type. A property with no VALUE parameter and no known default type MUST become a JSON string holding the unprocessed value text, with type unknown. Using text instead would cause extra escaping, which breaks round-tripping. An unrecognized parameter becomes a string holding its value text.

Going back, an unknown property MUST NOT get a VALUE parameter, and its value MUST be copied over without processing. For example, the jCal property x-complaint-deadline with type unknown and value 20110512T120000Z returns to X-COMPLAINT-DEADLINE:20110512T120000Z.
sections.eli5: When the translator meets a word it does not know, it does not guess. It copies the word exactly as it is and marks it unknown, so it can be put back perfectly later.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
jCal only translates between two formats with a one-to-one mapping. It does not change the meaning of the data or add or remove security considerations for it, and everything in Section 7 of RFC 5545 still applies.

JSON brings its own risks, discussed in Section 12 of RFC 7159. A flaw in a JSON parser could still be a threat, so a parser aware of these issues should be used. Passing jCal to the JavaScript evaluation function is called an unacceptable security risk, and a native JSON parser is preferred. The RFC also expects that the new format will spread iCalendar data more widely, for example into web applications.
sections.eli5: Changing the way a message is written does not change what it says, but you should open it with a careful tool, not one that runs anything it finds inside.

sections.title: Media Type and the UNKNOWN Value
sections.content:
The RFC registers the media type application/calendar+json, which SHOULD be used to transfer calendaring data in JSON. It takes the optional parameters method, component and optinfo defined for text/calendar in RFC 5545. Applications that use text/calendar, or application/json for calendar data, can use it as an alternative.

IANA also added UNKNOWN to the iCalendar value data types registry with the status Reserved - Do not use. It is reserved for jCal alone and MUST NOT appear in any iCalendar data.
sections.eli5: Every kind of file needs a name tag so programs know what it is. This gives calendar-in-JSON its own name tag, and keeps one special word off limits for everyone else.
